sections.title: Introduction: The Cultural Heart of Tswana Life
sections.content:
In Tswana culture, food is far more than mere sustenance—it is a central expression of identity, community, and tradition. The Setswana serving consists of a starch and protein, relish and a salad. Meals are communal affairs, shared among family and community members, and the preparation of food is often as significant as its consumption. Traditional ceremonies—weddings, funerals, initiation rites, and community gatherings—are all marked by the preparation and sharing of specific foods.

Batswana are mainly subsistence farmers and they pride themselves in their culture especially when it comes to food. The cuisine of Botswana is unique but shares some characteristics with other cuisines of Southern Africa. At its heart, Setswana cuisine is built around three pillars: starches (grains), proteins (particularly beef), and wild or cultivated vegetables and fruits.

sections.title: Part One: Staple Foods (Dijo tsa Setswana)

subsections.title: The Foundation of the Meal
subsections.content: Starches form the foundation of every Tswana meal. The typical meal consists of a stiff porridge or grain dish served with a protein and a relish. Setswana cuisine consists of, but is not limited to, maize meal, samp, sorghum, fat cakes, and mophane worms.

subsections.title: Pap / Phaleche (Maize Meal Porridge)
subsections.content:
Pap (also known as phaleche) is the most common staple food in Botswana. It is made from finely ground maize meal cooked with water until it reaches a stiff, dough-like consistency. Pap is the everyday starch that accompanies almost every meal—whether served with meat, vegetables, or stews. It is filling, inexpensive, and versatile.

There are different consistencies of pap:
- Stiff pap (bogobe or phaleche) – the thickest version, eaten with the hands and used to scoop up meat and relish
- Soft pap – a looser version, often eaten for breakfast or served to children and the sick

subsections.title: Bogobe (Sorghum Porridge)
subsections.content:
Bogobe is a porridge made from sorghum (mabele). Sorghum is a traditional grain that predates maize in Botswana and remains culturally significant. Bogobe can be prepared in several ways:
- Bogobe jwa lerotse – sorghum meal cooked with melon and sour milk. This is a special dish prepared at weddings and other important ceremonies. The melon is usually pre-prepared with sour milk and stored to be used whenever needed.
- Fermented sorghum porridge (Ting) – a sour, fermented porridge that is a delicacy
- Bogobe jwa mabele – plain sorghum porridge, often eaten with meat or sour milk

subsections.title: Samp (Setampa)
subsections.content:
Samp (setampa) is coarsely ground maize, similar to hominy. It is often:
- Cooked with beans to make dikgobe
- Eaten with pounded meat (seswaa) at weddings
- Served as a side dish with meat stews

Samp has a chewy texture and is more substantial than fine maize meal. It was historically a staple of the Tswana diet before the widespread adoption of refined maize meal.

subsections.title: Dikgobe
subsections.content: Dikgobe is a dish of samp mixed with beans. This combination of grains and legumes provides a complete protein and is a nutritious, filling meal. Different types of beans are grown locally, such as black beans, sugar beans, and kidney beans.

subsections.title: Other Starches
subsections.content:
- Sweet reed – a traditional starch source
- Ditloo, letlhodi, makgomane – traditional legumes and starches
- Groundnuts (manoko) – peanuts, often eaten as a snack or used in cooking

subsections.title: The Centrality of Cattle
subsections.content:
Cattle are deeply intertwined with the identity and pride of Batswana. Meat, specifically beef, plays a vital role in Tswana culture; it is present at all types of gatherings and is served in a variety of ways. A large quantity of high-quality organic beef is produced in Botswana, mainly because the culture is centered around cattle farming.

Beef is the most popular meat, followed by goat meat, sheep, and Tswana chicken. River fish are also part of Botswana cuisine, particularly in the Okavango Delta region.

subsections.title: Seswaa – The National Dish
subsections.content:
Seswaa (also known as chotlho or leswao) is a food unique to Botswana—salted, mashed-up meat. It is the national dish of Botswana and is a true Botswana classic.

Preparation: Seswaa consists of meat on the bone (usually beef) that is slow-cooked in salted water. The most common cuts are the shoulder, rib, rump, and neck. All parts of the cow are used but often cooked separately as they vary in toughness. The meat is traditionally prepared in a three-legged cast iron pot over an open fire. It is slow-cooked in water and lots of salt for an average of five hours. Once the meat has been cooked, it is pounded with large wooden pestles, then served over pap.

Cultural significance: Seswaa is a standard delicacy at most traditional events, including weddings and funerals. It is usually prepared by men due to the physical exertion during the preparation process. Some scholars have motivated for the recognition of seswaa as worthy of inscription under UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Seswaa is served with the traditional pap and side green vegetables, usually a local kind of spinach.

subsections.title: Segwapa (Biltong / Beef Jerky)
subsections.content:
Segwapa (also known as digwapa) is the Setswana name for dried meat or biltong. It is a popular method of preservation and consumption of beef that happens in the winter.

Preparation: Strips of meat are cut into string-like pieces, rubbed with salt and sometimes chili, and then air-dried. When meat is like this, it is called digwapa.

Cultural significance: Most Batswana make segwapa in their homes, especially in rural areas where there isn't any refrigeration to preserve meat. It is a flavorful meat dish where strips of meat are soaked in vinegar and then coated with a mix of salt and spices like coriander, cloves, and black pepper.

subsections.title: Mogatla (Oxtail Stew)
subsections.content:
Mogatla means 'oxtail' in Setswana. It is a stew that is savored all across Botswana and could be regarded as a national comfort food because of its deep ties with Botswana's culture.

Cultural significance: Most Batswana get their income from rearing and selling cattle, and they tend to save the less expensive cuts, such as the tail, for special occasions. Oxtail can take longer to cook, as half of its weight is bones and it has tougher meat, but once the juices and flavors of tomatoes, onions, broth, and bay leaves have been absorbed, the result is a delicious stew.

subsections.title: Tshotlo / Tlhakwana (Shredded Meat and Cow Heel)
subsections.content: Tshotlo is shredded meat, and Tlhakwana is cow heel or pork trotter. These are traditional dishes often served at special occasions. Seswaa, or chotlho or leswao, is a very popular traditional meat dish made for most special occasions.

subsections.title: Menoto (Chicken Feet)
subsections.content: Menoto is Setswana for 'chicken feet'. It is a common street food, usually roasted over a barbecue after being seasoned and spiced. Menoto is a popular food that many people prefer to eat hot. It can also be cooked into a stew to bring out its gelatin. In restaurants, they are served in large portions as chicken feet don't have much meat on their bones.

subsections.title: Serobe (Tripe)
subsections.content: Serobe is tripe—the intestines and some offal of goats, sheep, or cows. Sometimes trotters are featured in this dish. Mogodu is a combination of chopped serobe (tripe) and mala (intestines) served as a stew often with hot pap or dumpling.

subsections.title: Other Meats
subsections.content:
- Tswana chicken – free-range local chicken, highly valued for its flavour
- Lamb and mutton
- River fish – particularly in the Okavango Delta region

subsections.title: The Importance of Wild Foods
subsections.content:
Fifty-four (54) wild edible plants, most available after rains, were documented in a study of three Botswana villages. Fruits, roots, tubers, nuts, and leaves of wild edible plants are used in different forms—some as diet recipes, snacks, herbal tea, substrates, and as an inoculum source for fermented products.

There is a worry that the young generation has limited knowledge and skills to process indigenous foods, and unlike old days relying on indigenous foods, these days people buy imported processed foods and beverages from supermarkets. This represents a significant loss of traditional knowledge.

subsections.title: Mophane Worms (Mashonzha)
subsections.content:
Mophane worms are actually the caterpillar of the emperor moth (Gonimbrasia belina). They are a highly valued and economically important food source in Botswana.

Preparation: Mophane worms are cooked in hot ashes, boiled, or dried and fried. One recipe involves soaking dried mopane worms in hot water for about 2 hours, then cooking gently for 20 minutes.

Cultural significance: The mopane tree is the host plant for the mopane worm, making this insect a vital part of the food system in northern Botswana. They are a protein-rich food that is both nutritious and culturally significant.

subsections.title: Morogo (Wild Spinach)
subsections.content:
Morogo is the Setswana term for wild spinach or indigenous leafy vegetables. There are different varieties:
- Morogo wa dinawa – dried bean leaves
- Various indigenous leafy vegetables that grow wild and are available seasonally

Dried bean leaves are a popular Setswana food. These wild vegetables are an important source of micronutrients, such as iron, vitamin A (β-carotene) and zinc.

subsections.title: Wild Fruits
subsections.content:
Botswana is home to a variety of indigenous fruits:
- Marula (Sclerocarya birrea) – a fruit used to make beverages and enjoyed fresh
- Watermelons – believed to have originated in Botswana
- Moretlwa – raisin bush berries (from the Raisin Bush plant)
- Gau – fruit of the Mokolwane palm
- Englerophytum magalismontanum – a wild fruit used in the preparation of indigenous foods and traditional medicine
- Cooking melons – grown locally

A study conducted in Ramotswa village generated 50 wild edible plants among which 29 were wild fruits.

sections.title: Part Four: Vegetables and Side Dishes

subsections.title: Beans and Legumes
subsections.content:
Different types of beans are grown locally:
- Black beans
- Sugar beans
- Kidney beans
- Ditloo – traditional beans
- Letlhodi
- Makgomane

subsections.title: Morogo (Wild Spinach)
subsections.content: As mentioned above, morogo is a crucial part of the Tswana diet, providing essential nutrients and variety to meals.

subsections.title: Traditional Vegetables
subsections.content:
Traditional or indigenous leafy vegetables have been reported as an important source of micronutrients. These include:
- Amaranth (Amaranthus cruentus)
- Nightshade (Solanum scabrum)

subsections.title: Bojalwa ja Setswana (Traditional Sorghum Beer)
subsections.content:
Bojalwa ja Setswana is the traditional beer made from sorghum. It is one of the most widely mentioned indigenous beverages.

Cultural significance: Traditional beer is brewed for ceremonies and social gatherings. It is a central part of weddings, funerals, initiation ceremonies, and community celebrations. The brewing of traditional beer is a skill passed down through generations, primarily by women.

The results of a socio-economic study show that Traditional Beer (Bojalwa ja Setswana) is one of the alcoholic beverages predominantly produced across the districts of Botswana.

subsections.title: Khadi
subsections.content:
Khadi is a fermented drink made of water, berries/tubers, and brown sugar. It is another widely mentioned indigenous beverage.

Preparation: Khadi is made by fermenting water with berries, tubers, and brown sugar. It is a traditional beverage that varies in recipe and strength depending on the region and the ingredients available.

subsections.title: Chibuku
subsections.content: Chibuku is a commercial traditional beer made from Chibuku powder. It is produced across the districts of Botswana.

subsections.title: Gemere (Ginger Beer)
subsections.content: Gemere is ginger beer, the main non-alcoholic drink produced in all districts of Botswana. It is made using ginger powder and is usually left to ferment for a day or two. Home-made refreshing drinks using watermelon, marula fruit, or ginger powder are common.

subsections.title: Mageu
subsections.content: Mageu is a drink made by using leftover porridge and water. It is famous for serving to sick people as it is smooth and easily edible without having to chew but is nutritious. The name is derived from the process of allowing porridge to ferment.

subsections.title: Ila
subsections.content: Ila is an alcoholic beverage made from maize meal. It proved to be the most profitable among indigenous beverages in a recent study.

subsections.title: Setopoti / Chitopoti
subsections.content: Setopoti (or Chitopoti) is an alcoholic beverage produced from watermelon. It was produced in the highest volumes even though it was seasonal and had the highest amount of wastage.

subsections.title: Modaefok
subsections.content: Modaefok is another alcoholic beverage produced across the districts of Botswana.

subsections.title: Motjema / Motsema (Palm Wine)
subsections.content: Motjema (or motsema) is palm wine made from the sap of the Mokolwane palm. It is a traditional alcoholic beverage, particularly associated with the Okavango Delta region and the Wayeyi people.

sections.title: Part Six: Food Preservation and Processing
sections.content:
Batswana are skilled at food preservation. Traditional preservation methods include:
- Drying meat – cutting red meat into string-like pieces, rubbing it with salt and sometimes chili, and then air-drying it to make segwapa (biltong)
- Drying bean leaves – for use as morogo wa dinawa throughout the year
- Preserving melon – yellow melon is usually prepared with sour milk for preservation and kept in storage for future use
- Making mageu – from leftover porridge or pap
- Mokungwana – some tribes preserve spoiling or rotten meat by drying it to be used as relish for a long time

Processing Challenges:
Some beans and cereal grains take a long time to cook, leading to consumption of energy. Mould spoilage from inadequately dried products, presence of insects/pests, and soil impurities are also challenging. Because of high temperature and low rainfall, availability of some edible plants is scarce.

subsections.title: Okavango Delta Region
subsections.content:
- More fish in the diet due to the abundant waterways
- Mokolwane palm products (fruit, palm wine)
- Water-based foods and aquatic plants

subsections.title: Kalahari Region
subsections.content:
- More wild foods and game meat
- Drought-resistant crops like sorghum and millet
- Wild fruits and tubers adapted to arid conditions

subsections.title: Eastern Botswana (Central District)
subsections.content:
- Cattle-based cuisine – more beef and dairy products
- Maize and sorghum as staple starches
- Seswaa as the premier celebratory dish

sections.title: Part Eight: Cultural Significance of Food

subsections.title: Food and Social Status
subsections.content:
Cattle are not just a food source but a measure of wealth and status. Traditional ceremonies, especially weddings and funerals, involve the slaughtering of cattle. To bury a person without slaughtering their own cattle is considered a great shame.

A large amount of high-quality organic beef is produced in Botswana mainly because the culture is centered around cattle farming. Cattle represent years of hard work and perseverance. The size of a man's herd traditionally reflected his status in the community, a mark of dignity.

subsections.title: Food and Ceremony
subsections.content:
- Weddings – seswaa, bogobe jwa lerotse, samp, and traditional beer are central
- Funerals – cattle are slaughtered to feed guests; seswaa is a standard dish
- Initiation ceremonies – specific foods are prepared for the initiates and the community
- Community gatherings – food is shared as an expression of botho (ubuntu)

subsections.title: Food and Gender
subsections.content:
- Seswaa is usually prepared by men due to the physical exertion during the preparation process
- Brewing traditional beer is primarily a women's responsibility
- Cooking for ceremonies often involves gender-based division of labour

subsections.title: The Impact of Urbanisation
subsections.content:
Urbanisation has led to changes in food practices:
- Imported processed foods are increasingly replacing traditional foods in urban areas
- Young people have limited knowledge and skills to process indigenous foods
- Supermarkets are replacing traditional markets
- Western diets are becoming more common, especially among the urban elite

subsections.title: The Impact of Climate
subsections.content: Because of high temperature and low rainfall, availability of some edible plants is scarce. Climate change poses a threat to traditional food systems, particularly wild foods that depend on seasonal rains.

subsections.title: The Resilience of Tradition
subsections.content:
Despite these challenges, traditional foods remain central to Tswana identity:
- Seswaa is still served at all major ceremonies
- Traditional beer continues to be brewed for celebrations
- Mophane worms remain a delicacy
- Cattle remain the measure of wealth and status
- Food preservation techniques are still practised in rural areas

subsections.title: The Case for Recognition
subsections.content: Some scholars have motivated for the recognition of seswaa, a beef-related cuisine, as worthy of inscription under UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage. This reflects growing recognition of the cultural value of Botswana's traditional foods and the need to document and preserve food heritage.
